newsitem.title: USA: Clinton embraces air safety proposals.
newsitem.headline: Clinton embraces air safety proposals.

text.p: Acting to ease public qualms about U.S. air safety, President Bill Clinton on Wednesday accepted the proposals of a White House commission aimed at cutting the rate of fatal air accidents by 80 percent over 10 years.

The commission began its deliberations at Clinton's request after a string of plane crashes in 1996, including the Valujet disaster in Florida and the still-unexplained TWA Flight 800 crash shortly after takeoff from New York's Kennedy Airport.

Vice President Al Gore, who chaired the blue-ribbon panel, said as he gave Clinton its half-inch thick report that "we call on government and industry to work together to cut the fatal accident rate of aviation by 80 percent in 10 years."

"This whole report is a blueprint for action. We do have the safest aviation system in the world. But as we look to the next century and see the doubling of traffic that's going to take place over the next 20 years, we know that we have to do even better," Gore said.

His panel, which included aviation officials and private citizens whose relatives died in recent air disasters, called for speeding up the modernisation of the U.S. air traffic control system and intensifying the fight against terrorism. It also offered specific proposals for reaching these goals.

It said aviation security was a national security issue and the federal governent should provide "substantial funding" for capital improvements linked to safety. It urged spending $100 million a year on capital requirements identified by the Federal Aviation Administration.

Elaine Kamarck, an aide to the vice president, said that implementing the commission's recommendations would not increase overall government outlays in the near term because all of the money for the programme was already budgeted.
"We feel that there is adequate funding to do all the things in this report," Kamarck told reporters.
The panel recommended that the FAA draw up a plan within six months for developing by the year 2005 a satellite-based air traffic control system to update the current ground-based system.
To combat terror, it recommended that a "bag match" system linked to selecting, or "profiling" passengers be implemented no later than December of this year.
This would mean that a bag that had not been screened and that belonged to a passenger selected for extra scrutiny would not be allowed on board a plane.
The panel said the U.S. Postal Service should be given the authority to screen suspicious mail, and randomly screen all mail weighing over a pound for potential explosive devices.

The commission commended an airline industry initiative to equip cargo holds of passenger aircraft with smoke detectors, a matter that was an issue in the crash of a Valujet plane near Miami last May in which 110 lives were lost.
"The recommendations in this report are strong and we will put them into action," Clinton said, vowing to use all the tools of modern science to make flying as safe as possible.

He said the National Aeronautics and Space Administration would aid the air safety improvement effort by spending $500 million on research and development over five years "to make sure we do achieve our accident reduction goal."

Much of the money will come from a $1 billion anti-terrorism programme that Clinton signed into law in October 1996. That spending was approved after the panel issued its preliminary report last September.
Clinton said the government was already installing 54 highly sophisticated bomb detection machines at key airports and training and deploying over 100 bomb sniffing dog teams.

He also said that the Federal Aviation Administration was hiring 300 new agents to test airport security, and that the FBI was adding 644 new agents and 620 support personnel to bolster its counter-terrorism efforts.

"We are taking action to make our people more secure, but we cannot afford to rest," Clinton said, adding that the new budget he sent to Congress last week provides $100 million for future aviation safety improvements.
